My first Edward Yang film, and while the story itself is relatively clear about Taiwan’s situation during the period it portrays, the aftermath of the Chinese Civil War, the migration to the island, and the way violence, prejudice, and social tensions shaped that society, the way the film chooses to tell all of this feels far more fragmented and disorienting. At first, it seems as though we will follow a single character in something close to a coming-of-age story, especially through his feelings for a girl. But over the course of its four-hour runtime, the film constantly branches out into teenage power disputes, gang rivalries, side characters, and parallel stories that do not always clearly converge with the main narrative. This also extends to Yang ’s mise-en-scène. Many of the film’s most important moments avoid the traditional shot-reverse-shot structure; the camera often remains static, refusing to follow reactions or decisive actions, leaving much of what happens outside the frame, almost as mere suggestion. It’s an interesting style because it forces the viewer to fill in the gaps through their own perception, yet at the same time it dissipates some of the dramatic weight of the events and weakens the emotional involvement with what the characters are going through.

I had to watch this giant Taiwanese film for an upcoming podcast. My cohost loved it, which put a bit more pressure on me to at least tolerate it. But here's the thing. No movie justifies a four hour run time. Nothing. Even if Batman and Spider-Man were fighting an army of fully nude clones all played by Sydney Sweeney, I'd start looking at my watch after the third hour. A Bright Summer Day isn't just crazy long. It's boring. It's a slice of life movie, which I generally despise. So, this was never gonna win me over. I had trouble latching onto the plot, if there even was one. It follows a kid in Taipei who starts flunking school because he's getting involved in a gang, I think. There's also a movie being filmed nearby, but that doesn't really go anywhere. The kid gets increasingly angry towards the world, particularly anyone who's into the girl he's into. That bitterness and lack of communication explodes in a violent outburst that lands him in prison. That's the gist. You tell me if you think that takes four hours to relay? A Brighter Summer Day is my third Edward Yang film after Taipei Story and Yi Yi . I didn't like any of them, but I liked this one the least. It's way too damn long, it's dull, it barely has a plot, and watching it felt like putting in a shift. Definitely not my thing.

While this film has been on my to-watch list for a very long time, as well as being one of the highest rated films here on Letterboxd, two things kept me from diving right in: its four hour runtime and the fact that I really did not like "Yi Yi", the only other movie I'd seen directed by Edward Yang. I finally did watch this and it's official: I do not like Edward Yang's movies. This film was, to me, unwatchable - though for some inexplicable reason, I sat through the whole, excruciating thing. The movie is about a family living in Taiwan during 1959-1960, and centers on one of the children, Si'r, who is a middle schooler. There are teenage street gangs, there is dating, there is secret police, there are economic problems, and I could not have been more bored or less interested. Whatever definition anyone may have of a flashy filmmaker, Yang is the polar opposite. The camera barely moves, shots are long and drawn out even when nothing is happening, the framing is wide and at a remove. Most of the cast is made up of non-professional actors, and it really shows, as the acting is mediocre to downright bad. If there is a logical plot, it was completely lost on me. But the worst thing about this film is its protagonist. I don't know if it was by design or because of the actor's terrible skills, but Si'r is so absent, so vacant, and so blank of a character, passive doesn't even begin to articulate it, that there is nowhere for a viewer to enter the film. We don't know how to feel or what to care about or what is happening internally because Si'r, and really every character in the whole damn movie, have zero expressions, do not react to anything going on, even deaths and murders, and their motivations remain completely unknowable. Look, I am so beyond in the minority here, but I have studied cinema, I teach cinema and have done so for two decades, I help run an independent movie theater and even host a monthly foreign film series... Heck, I freaking lived in Asia and have been to Taiwan. I am not some dummy ignoramus who doesn't understand cinema or art-house films. And yet, I hated this with all my heart. I don't know what it could possibly be about this film that has captured people's hearts over the years. I have to wonder if people feel the need to justify sitting through something so long and reward it so they don't feel like they've wasted four hours of their lives, hence rating it higher than it deserves. Either way, I did not like this movie at all, and am as entitled to that reaction as are those that love it. But boy oh boy, did I not like this. At all. Grade: D

How do you rate a movie that’s both amazing and terrible at the same time? There’s a terrific scene 42 min into the movie where Si’r’s brother, Lao Er, goes to play pool at the 217 gang’s hideout. Although we don’t actually see him playing pool, we hear him pocketing every shot and see the looks of surprise on a spectator’s face as he wins the game, and all of the money on the table. This is a great scene, but it’s also confusing: we never actually see Lao Er’s face, and have to intuit that it’s him based on a brief scene 20 minutes prior in which he picks up a cue ball at a party. You would also think this foreshadows him winning lots of money playing pool (given his incredible talent) but the next significant time we see him, it’s towards the end of the film when he’s being beaten over debt he’s accrued from gambling—something that feels inconsistent with his previous characterization. I mention this scene because it represents what I dislike so much about this film. It’s filled with scenes that are so great on their own, but within the context of the broader narrative, fail to coalesce into anything cohesive. Toward the end, it’s revealed that Si’r actually saw Ming kissing Sly, not Jade. This ultimately leads to the climax of the film, so it’s undoubtedly an important piece of information. But it was never clear to the audience that Si’r thought it was Jade who kissed Sly in the first place, so this detail really just adds confusion. And that initial kissing scene is briefer than the pool scene I mentioned earlier, so it’s narrative weight isn’t clear either. I wanted to enjoyed this movie more than I did, but instead found myself constantly pausing and rewinding to understand what was happening in the story, and because of this, I never forgot that I was watching a movie. And after it was over, I wished that I could forget it.

It has all the qualities of a tv-series, its long meandering and with several storylines, and a camera-work that emphasizes the sets and faces, and it has no cinematic qualities, such as impressive camera-work, dramatic hooks etc… This sometimes happend before the great tv-series explosion in the 21st century. Great quality scripts that today would be considered tv series could be produced, and people thought they were awesome (Heimat, Best of Youth are two examples), but today you can feel that they are in a different category. This would 100% be made as a tv series if it had been made after 2000. And so, I think it should be compared with other tv series. That would also explain it’s high ratings: tv series are generally higher rates than movies.

I don’t care that it’s four hours long or deliberately paced; I wasn’t bored or checking the clock every few minutes. It’s just that, in the end, so little happens that I was left wondering why we needed four hours to tell this story. I suppose fans would say therein lies the brilliance. Different strokes. I found the lead character Si’r maddenly dull and frankly didn’t understand his “what am I rebelling against? Whaddya got?” character any more at minute 230-something than I did at minute one. His problems, albeit colored by the specifics of the Taiwanese/Mainland conflict, are the same problems that have dogged teenagers from different cultures for many years. I just didn’t find him compelling enough to follow for four hours (I would have gladly traded this for a Cat movie following his attempts to be a singer of American rock songs. I kept waiting for the moment when he hit puberty and could no longer sing the Connie Francis parts). I also thought that given the extended run time too much was rushed, brushed aside, or given short shrift. The movie studio doesn’t add anything to the story; Honey is discussed in hushed, reverent tones and when he finally shows up doesn’t do much of anything other than act as a catalyst for one of the film’s better sequences; Ma is also given a build up but disappears for swathes of the movie and, again, doesn’t live up to the hype; the middle sister is such a non-character that I thought she was a maid or family friend until she’s finally given something to do in the last twenty minutes; Cat’s rock band disappears when the rented hall is no longer needed as a story beat; Sly disappears from the story and later reappears as a completely changed person and talks about the past as if years have gone by but it’s actually only been maybe months. I just think given the deliberation that there should not have been so many loose ends and unexplored avenues. I wish I vibed with this the way everyone else does, but it left me cold.

C'est ce genre de film que je regrette de ne pas avoir assez apprécié et où j'ai un sentiment de déception entre ce que l'on m'a vendu : "le grand chef d'œuvre d'Edward Yang ", "meilleur que Yi-Yi", "fresque profonde de la société taïwanaise en crise durant le milieu du XXe siècle" Il n'en fut rien. Le film à beaucoup de qualités, l'ambiance est au rendez-vous, certains éléments sonores, matériels, sont marquants, mais pour le reste... La première moitié du film est plutôt agréable et bien exécutés, mais en 4h de film on ne voit aucune évolution dans les personnages quasiment. C'est peut-être aussi une volonté du réalisateur, où le film se termine avec la voix de la radio qui introduisait le film justement. J'ai bien aimé Mao , j'ai apprécié le trop peu de temps de Honey a l'écran qui a suscité un vif intérêt chez moi très rapidement. Mais le personnage principal, sa romance avec Ming , ses interactions amicales, familiales, scolaires, au sein de son gang, bah franchement de marbre. J'ai tellement préféré suivre Mao et sa transcription des musiques d'Elvis Presley , ou du père de famille, réfugié politique chinois, que du personnage principal qui ne m'a rien évoqué. Même la fin qui est choquante, est niaise. Edward Yang est fort pour nous montrer un personnage frustré, avec le syndrome du sauveur, qui veut sauver tout le monde alors que c'est lui qui devrait être sauvé. De ce point de vue là, Yang a réussi son pari de créer un personnage qui en 4h à l'écran n'évolue absolument pas. Si’r a été trop souvent séparé de toute forme d’amitié et de stabilité. Sa vie n'est que gang et violence, de ce point de vue là, le réalisateur réussi à créer un personnage insensible, mais même comme ça, ça ne m'a pas parlé. Si on devait évoquer les points forts ce seraient les 3 personnages que j'ai évoqués avant ( Mao, Honey , le père) et l'ambiance automnale des plans. Ma première déception au bout de 2h de visionnage c'est vraiment le fait que le contexte historique et politique ne soit pas aussi prégnant dans le récit. On voit les tensions de la société taïwanaise qui laisse sa jeunesse en recherche d'identités et répond à ça par la violence, la constitution de gang et des conflits territoriaux. On voit à un moment un bref interrogatoire de la police secrète qui suspecte des potentiels infiltrer communistes mais en dehors de ça, c'est le vide. Ça ne m'a pas parlé. Certains plans, notamment dans la salle des fêtes, avec les néons sous la pluie sont vraiment magnifiques, énormément de très beaux plans, Yang ne me déçois jamais sur ce plan-là. Pour le reste, scénario, contexte historique, personnages, ambiance sonore... J'ai été déçu. Peut-être trop d'attente. J'attends de voir " A Confucian Confusion ", j'ai très peur d'être déçu aussi, à voir. « Je ne crains que deux sortes de gens Shandong. Ceux qui n'ont pas peur de mourir, et ceux qui n'ont pas d'honneur. Où tu te situes ? »

Couldn't get into this at all! It's directed by a tortoise. Everything is so sleepy and heavy, and framed in a way that blocks it off or makes it look small. The whole style draws attention to itself, puts you at a distance, and makes it hard to care about what's happening. Naturalistic acting combined with very stagey direction makes it completely uninvolving - and ultimately boring. It's guarded, and emotionally muted most of the way through. The film seems more interesting in indulging in the quality of its craft, and the importance of its themes, rather than taking you on an emotional journey. All head and no heart. Not a good idea for something so long, and so technically sterile! In spite of all that, there are things to like. A coming of age story is always a winner, gets you feeling all wistful. Seeing people live their normal lives with horrible war and crime in the background is always a provocative contrast, especially when you see kids having to think and act like adults. Plus shots of trees rustling on sunny days are always nice to see. There's lots of dependable, crowd pleasing stuff in here. Packaging that stuff in a highbrow, semi-ambient epic doesn't detract from it, and doesn't enhance it either, it just drags it out. (Spoilers ahead) The final bit is very good, and the ending is a great gut-punch. But we could have got there much quicker for the same payoff - if not a better one!! It's basically Jeanne Dielman isn't it, but even longer. Much less constrained than that film, but much less tense as a result. Dielman's power comes from its austerity of both style and substance - it withholds everything until you start to go insane! BSD is austere in style (long and slow and quiet) but not in plot: there's lots of characters doing lots of things, so rather than tension ratcheting up as the runtime runs on, it feels instead like you're meandering, lazily circling around the same ideas over and over again. BSD tries to be too many things - an art film, a crime drama, a meditation on youth and lost innocence, a social commentary, a true story - it sprawls out in so many directions and ultimately exhausts itself. When you give the audience this much, what are they supposed to take away? The shocking final moments are my takeaway, and they're so shocking that they kind of override everything that comes before. Which begs the question - why spend all that time building up to such a sudden climax? The answer, I think, is to make the climax feel even more significant than it is. The movie isn't this long because it has to be, it's this long because the director doesn't seem to know about economy, about covering large distances in small steps, about cooking all your ingredients down into small rich bites. I'm full of raw vegetables, a whole table full, and all I'll remember is the great big fart that comes at the end...

Week 3 - A film from Taiwan Clearly made with expertise, passion and care. Yang's eye for framing is brilliant - visually making the most of what's presented. But. And it's a big but. There simply isn't enough coherent narrative or likeable characters to sustain one's interest for 4 hours.  A slow burn is fine but not over this time. I suspect that those who speak the language and understand the history (or make more efforts to do so than I) will get so much more from this than I did. Yang not only makes few concessions to an international / uninformed audience about context, he makes it hard to understand who the many side characters are, especially when they are rarely addressed by name in a scene ( and had nicknames). It seems reductive to say that there's a very good 2 hour film in here - but that's how I have rated. It was a slog, technically excellent, but ultimately disappointing.

Fanny & Alexander by Bergman is 5 hours long, 1 hour longer than ABSD, and it does not feel this tedious. I’m cool with slice of life movies, I’m cool with movies that wander, as long as I care about the characters and feel engaged. But it felt very unfocused. I’m not left caring deeply about anyone or anything in particular. The characters didn’t feel very fleshed out or developed. The film stuffs so many characters in one that it’s hard to truly connect with anybody. Also, some of Yang’s weakest writing for his female characters. Overall, the film’s size doesn’t match the size of emotion and connection that it elicits. It’s an investment with minimal returns.

It often feels as if they’re being pushed by the script rather than driven by believable intentions. The four-hour runtime isn’t the problem. Note: I more than likely no longer agree with this review, but I will not know until I rewatch. I hate watching a grand epic like this and leaving it feeling relatively unaffected by it outside of the ending, but that was the case here. My main gripe overall is that I never got the sense that Ming was a character in her own right. She felt entirely defined by her relationships to other men, which did work to drive the development of people like Sly, Ma, Honey, Tiger, and obviously Si'r, but ended up leaving me overall unconvinced in the relationship and the fact that he would care enough for the ending to go the way it does. I would have loved more of a lens into Ming's life, what we get about her family would always pull me back and I think that an expansion on that and her thoughts on the screen test would have made her feel more three-dimensional. I greatly enjoyed a large majority of the cinematography, especially when they would use repeated visual motifs in a slightly altered way to show what all has changed through time, but did somewhat struggle with the lighting in a large number of the nighttime scenes. I was already struggling to keep track of the large cast as is, so when the details of who was who would be obscured by the dark I would tend to get lost in my own head trying to unravel who was doing what (I'm still not quite sure I know who Airplane is lmao). Loved the performances though, seeing so many young and amateur actors do so well was incredible. Overall, I feel as if my relative apathy to this is almost a personal failing, and hope that in the inevitable rewatch I do when my thoughts fade away I come away with a more positive perspective.

the thing i often find the most frustrating about writing, especially writing fiction with intention of having it published, is the inability to compress the totality of your work and what you're trying to say into something that could hook others in a few minutes as effectively as staring at a canvas or listening to a song. all art forms have a relation to space and time, and how they are engaged with by others in space and time, but differ in the amount of control they have over either or both of those things: a sculpture informs a space, and remains in time, but it can't control if someone walks past it without looking, or the lobby it's located in decides to carve it into pieces and stash it in a warehouse; movies and songs have a completeness of time given that the time it takes you to engage with it is set by the artist, and while movies ideally inform the made-for-purpose space of the theater, and music finds intention of space in both the recording studio and the concert hall, nowadays with device proliferation both lack of control over the space where one watches or listens to it, and often have to share space with the "real" world beyond them; books are finite objects, but have no concrete power to exercise over you when it comes to how long it takes you to read them, where you read them, the quantity of sessions it takes to read them to completion and if you even finish them at all. with some new friends i took a trip to the noguchi museum the other day, which was in the final week of a special exhibition about the works of isamu noguchi specific to new york city, most of which were unrealized, destroyed or altered public works projects. i hadn't found a special exhibition that moving since the gustave caillebotte one at the art institute of chicago , mainly due to how starkly it contrasted with the solemnity and quiet and inscrutability and general rick-owens-runway-backgrounding of the permanent arrangement of the sculptures downstairs: here was a man who committed himself deeply to a city and believed in the transformative potential of labor, only to be rejected in most of his attempts to engender some productive change in his city vis a vis of planned public parks, playgrounds and general art spaces, a lifetime of fighting past this frustration informing the difficulty in "getting" the works downstairs without aide of museum copy, and the intention behind the bespokeness of the museum itself as noguchi's "final gift" to the city. on the train back home one of these new friends (all three of which being musicians, historically the type of artist bonnie is the farthest pole away from in terms of mutual understanding about our art practice and the mechanics behind it) expressed her own frustration at how noguchi's sculpture, and sculpture/museum works of visual art in general, stand so immediately and completely for themselves in a way that music doesn't, to which i laugh and said something to the effect of, "you musicians can achieve something for someone in three minutes what writing would take in three hours!" this was to be the first time i watched a brigher summer day in one continuous sitting (the first time i turned it on too late i got too tired after the first hour, and my first complete viewing was broken up with some pauses here and there), and in a theater, so given the profundity of the day prior at the noguchi, i was expecting to have another totality of artistic experience with a movie already quite dear to me, but four hours came and went and it never fully clicked into place for me, my favorite shots (the lacquered door, honey's entrance, the parallel bike walks between father and son, ming and si'r in the wheat fields, etc) seeming fixed and static. i found myself thinking about nashville , something with a similar quantity of moving parts that fall into place in a final act of public murder, and how the first time i saw nashville in a theater, also a rewatch, my heart could not stop pounding knowing someone was going to die soon and the fact it wouldn't be a surprise this time made it wrench the gut all the more, but a frustration i had with this the first time around that compounded even more here is that the development in si'r's character as acting on a capacity to kill someone is an exponential incongruity compared to the otherwise steady downs and rebounded ups and again downs of the narrative. yang in general is a historical example of mine of a male director with a great sensitivity towards fully realizing female characters, but the women in brighter summer day , despite the gender roles of the point in depicted space and time they occupy, are mostly instrumental and fall in and out of the narrative as needed. granted, this more than any of yang's other films is a Movie About Boys, and certain choices are smart ones, like how ming maintains a strong presence despite a lot of the information presented about her being skewed hearsay from boys and men who are invariably in love with her (beyond the retroactively-revealed-to-be-her flashlighted kiss at the start, we never actually see her *do* any of the fooling around the boys constantly claim of her), but, in the film paced like a three-hour gang epic with an hour rider of bildungsroman family drama at the end, her death, and the perceived necessity of it as a cementing of sir's arc, is perhaps the most senseless in a movie where a handful of teenagers die by the circumstance of samurai sword in near-total darkness. brighter summer day still remains to me one of yang's three works that achieve objective perfection in their filmmaking ( yi yi and a confucian confusion the other two), which i think only makes the flaws to its airtight seals all the more compelling. there has to be a critic out there who's said it better than me but i believe as some sort of universal law that as an artist gets older their work only becomes more and more about their art form of choice itself. consider the next-door movie studio here: it's certainly a space of frustration—the color of the dress is wrong, the actress isn't good enough, ming doesn't find si'r up in the rafters looking back at her—but the scenes here bookend the film in a way, given that si'r's decision to steal the flashlight is what ends up catching sly in the act, which many characters labor to tell si'r as the thing that started the whole mess, and si'r's decision to leave the flashlight back where he found it and replace it in his waistband with the knife the thing that kills ming, kills himself and the narrative in essence: film itself brings this story into existence, and ends it just as suddenly. ( jonathan rosenbaum's piece on yang writes about the flashlight better than i and reading it on the way to the screening really clued me to look out for it in all scenes like a video game key item.) it’s almost like in precisely mapping out every inch of the screen, in taking four years to prepare the filming of such a calibrated machine, yang took it to the limit only to find himself at the fundamental frustration that a limit is something you can never pass beyond; you can only keep making more things and infinitely continue to move forward. brighter summer day 's glass half-emptiness certainly leaves almost no way out for most of its characters—ming and honey are dead, ma loses his best friend, cat's tapes are trashed, si'r is jailed, si'r's father is reduced to a paranoid wifebeater with no promising future employment, si'r's mother is left with an absence she can never fill despite how close she holds it to herself, lao er is without hopes or dreams, even the reverend of the church to which si'r's middle sister devotes herself seems to hold her in some minor disdain—but the one character who seems to have it good in his final scene, uncle fat, is in high spirits because of how si'r saved his life, regardless of si'r's prior expressed want to hurt him. i don't think si'r is particularly a stand-in for yang, as it's based on a real event he had some proximity to in his schoolboy days, but maybe si'r is a version of yang with a similar childhood interest in and proximity to a film, but a version of yang who could not overcome his frustrations, unaware to the fact that regardless of his possible intention to hurt uncle fat that night, something he did saved his life, and uncle fat has a renewed lease on life because of it. so regardless of how frustrating writing is for me, regardless of how frustrating it is to ever make anything, or even do anything, we only do it, we always do it to help someone live just a little longer.

The film does have its highlights. I like the stuff with the gangs and I like the issues surrounding the political and rock n roll connections coupled with a touch of identity. But the film is so long that trying to focus on them is difficult. Overall I'm glad I saw it and appreciate it a little better. But I still found it slow, overly long, and off focus. Let me start this review by saying that I anticipated this film so much before going in. I wanted to connect and emotionally stay with it for a while. For that reason, I began watching A Brighter Summer Day in a very "give the benefit of every doubt you have" kind of way. Hell, for the first hour, in which we get introduced to gangs and an ever-expanding cast, whenever I felt lost in what was going on, I thought it was me, not the film. But after four hours of what unfolded, I can confidently say it's rather the film. Yet I still feel sorry that I somehow couldn't make the most out of it. To say that this film is ambitious is an understatement. It certainly is, not only because of the epic scope of its characters or the '60s Taiwanese atmosphere it captures, which brings the first wave of Chinese settlers and reeks of a sort of chaos that combines an effort to remain strict while losing total control. Its ambition stems from the fact that it gives you an overwhelmingly full plot involving multiple gangs and several key characters, while trying to maintain a slice-of-life flow, especially when it comes to the main character, Si'r. The thing that I see most here is that this effort is appreciated and impresses a lot of people. And that may be a general criticism regarding films that last 4+ hours; I think people give too much credit to the sheer epicness of it all. But that doesn't necessarily mean the execution works neatly, and here it certainly doesn't. First of all, following what is going on in the first quarter is overwhelming. For example, an apparently important plot point is an encounter involving a kiss between two key people, yet we barely get a glance at it, and it's the characters reminding us about it that activate the flow of events. So many characters and angles are thrown at us, as if we had already been introduced to them an hour before. And I don't think the film is trying to play catch-up with us; it's more of an inclination that suggests we intuitively know or understand more. But we don't. Yet through all this, there are quite a few magical shots that trigger emotions right away. Angel Baby is an example of that, and Si'r and Ming's escape into the shooting field is another. In scenes like these, A Brighter Summer Day surely works and promises you more. But the continuity is so poor here. We get a big gang shootout, then immediately move on to the Secret Police plotline involving Si'r's dad, as if these two events connect to each other, except they don't. And that is where the ambitious nature loses me, because it doesn't impress me. Whenever I start to feel hooked, the film gets even greedier and throws something else at me. You feel the length here not because it's all too boring, nothing happens, and it's just dull; you feel it because there exists a contrast between a plot that is overwhelmingly full while being emotionally underwhelming. Si'r is a character who carries true potential for connection, yet he is too lost in the midst of everything, so while his ending looks powerful, his psychology becomes somewhat scattered the further the film goes. Ming is a rather consistent character, yet what we get from her are mostly glimpses, so she is wasted too. If I may count him as a key character, I think Honey's story is the most interesting one, and his ending is perhaps the most powerful section of the film. His shadow is what carries the back half of it, especially for Si'r and Ming, but for everybody else as well. Thus, the one thing A Brighter Summer Day does flawlessly is Honey: his mythic build-up and then the few encounters we have with him. Also, looking back at the first half—where I was still a hopeful believer in it—there is too much repetitive turf fighting that becomes meandering real quick. It stales things out and goes on and on. My main issue is not the length of the film, but it surely could have been tighter. Or perhaps it could have stayed the same length, but with less action and more introduction? Still, I can't say I disliked the entire thing; it's just that I expected much more. And the fact that there are glimpses of having that connection, the reminiscence of Yi Yi's genuine, minimalistic realism, just not being able to build through and through, is what hurts more. I am pretty sure a rewatch would favor this slightly. But at the moment, A Brighter Summer Day is a trying of an epic slice of life that places its most genuine focus on Si'r; yet I would argue that it never truly becomes a slice, and never a true intersection. It is a constant zoom in and zoom out, and you come across a lot of impressive pictures along the way. But much of it remains a big blur. Perhaps for some people that blur becomes a beautiful haze, or they simply can see through the fog better than I can. I tried, but it wasn't a particularly bright summer day. Between the film itself and the day I watched it—which indeed wasn't a bright summer day—I fault the film more.

For my hundredth film this year, I wanted to choose something special. I thought for a long time - maybe I should watch something iconic that I missed or haven’t gotten around to yet, or something that has been on my watchlist for a long time. But in the end, I decided to find a list of the longest films that are a must-watch. I don’t know why, but my eye fell on Edward Yang’s “A Brighter Summer Day” . And it seems to be the most monotonous multi-genre movie ever created . I read how people admire this film and call it one of their favorites. I read about where the idea for the film originally came from and what its main theme is. There are few answers, the movie is indeed not easy for an evening watch. The four-hour runtime really feels like four hours . It’s not entertaining, more like something meditative, thanks to its beautiful locations and shots. But at the same time, I got tired of it - tired of the changing subjects, of not understanding why I’m watching this now, why this person sits silently at a table for two minutes and I’m just observing. The film often references War and Peace (about three times), and we know Tolstoy is famous for his long descriptions of nature and so on, and while that is interesting and necessary in the novel, here it could be done without. The story itself is unsurprising despite the loglines and headlines, about the murder of a girl and a KGB investigation. Because of the slow pace, I don’t feel any emotions, they just show me events as if silently, and I take note of them without much surprise or sympathy. Usually I really do love long films, but I want the length to be justified, and here I didn’t notice that. Maybe I’m not smart enough to see the uniqueness and importance of this film, but it just didn’t resonate with me.

Wanted to connect with this the way I did with Yi Yi , but alas. Regardless, it’s a thorough restoration from Criterion that does justice to Yang’s vision. The guy was a creative visionary, no doubt about it. This epic pushes 4 hours with a focus on the lives of the Taiwanese children of Chinese expats/refugees fleeing mainland China after the Civil War. Though one could be mistaken in thinking the gang ‘turf war’ is only nominally a “war”, Yang disabuses us of that notion as he captures dramatic scenes of street violence, targeted hits on youth leaders and juvenile delinquency of all forms. The kids are abused and neglected at home, and they re-assert familiar power structures in the *playgrounds (*the tennis court, the music hall, the restaurant). Yang’s only music comes in diegetic form via ‘50s Western rock ‘n roll hits and sappy love ballads from Ricky Nelson to Elvis whom the characters adore. It’s a tapestry of a specific place during a specific moment in time under unique political circumstances, but for me, Yang seems unable to bridge the knowledge gap with the audience enough to make me care, especially given this runs at a punishingly languid pace.

This is a beautifully shot and undeniably impressive feat of filmmaking that a younger version of myself might have tried to find a way to love more than I actually did, but I've recently become a lot more cynical of these long, slow arthouse classics and I simply didn't emotionally connect with this one at all. I couldn't really find enough to latch onto in terms of story or character, and without those things you really start to feel every minute of the almost four-hour runtime. Gorgeous visuals alone weren't enough to make me love it.

My hot take? This is Burning but worse and in double the time. (Okay, I know that's being pretty reductive about both films, but that's my immediate reaction now the credits have finished and this is my crappy Letterboxd account so I'll do as I please.) While technically outstanding, I can't say I especially rate A Brighter Summer Day . Many seem to praise its sprawling, “novelistic” style but I'm in the minority here saying that works against the film, which would be much better served with a sharper focus. Praise the 100+ speaking parts all you want, but three hours in my partner and I were still saying things like, “Which boy is Airplane again?” There are too many little distractions taking away from what's really important. On that note, the card at the start telling you that youths are starting gangs because of a lack of identity and security does a lot of heavy lifting, because Yang doesn't show any of that. I know the director has more filmmaking talent in a speck of his dandruff than I do in my entire body, but I still think this is a failing of his and the film. (The kids singing songs in English doesn't scream identity crisis for me, sorry. People all around the world enjoy songs not in their native language – you could probably draw a historical line from Italian and Germanic operas all the way to K-pop to demonstrate this point – so this argument doesn't hold much weight for me, sorry.) Lastly, I have issues with both S'ir and Ming that affect my view of the film. It's tough to discuss without spoilers but I was shaking my head at both come the end. I think we're given too little insight into S'ir's interiority to really, let's say, “appreciate” what comes at the film's climax. Perhaps Yang wants us to be shocked/frustrated/confused by A Brighter Summer Day's seemingly irrational outcome, but without sufficient context, it lacks impact.

This is the longest film I've logged on Letterboxd and possibly the longest film I've ever seen. To direct a film of this magnitude is a monumental challenge, as maintaining great storytelling and cinematography for four hours is no easy feat. The power of a film with such proportions is that there is more time to get to know the cast and to see them grow, so that whatever the emotional payoff is at the climax, it is that much stronger. In A Brighter Summer Day, there is that intense payoff at the film's climax which is clearly aided by the large cast of characters we get to know, but the journey up to the last hour is far from perfect. The first director that makes me think of the word auteur. This is only the 2nd film I've seen apart from YiYi and you can really tell that he focuses on bringing a slice of life structure to the screen. Instead of telling stories where you can make a decent guess on where it's going and where it'll end up, he brings you smack in the middle of their messy reality and have you be an observer to a slow basic day in the life or a tense, highly emotional wave of feelings. This had a twist I wasn't expecting in the slightest and I enjoyed every moment.

I don't know why I was surprised given the subject matter throughout the film but the darkness of the concluding act of this film really devastated me. Maybe it's just because Yang's style is so disarmingly peaceful, with the whole film being wrapped in this daydreamy, nostalgic, hang-out movie glaze, or maybe it's because the film captures this feeling of an ephemeral period of time, with most of its subjects unjustly victimized by their era and circumstances, but regardless, it's extremely moving. You really get to live and breathe with his characters and even though there's this sort of transitory feel to their presence in the film, with fairly important characters being introduced or leaving with very little warning, you feel the time passing very clearly and experience the deep intensity of their growth and losses. That's why the ending just sucks you in, because by that point, you're not ready to leave these people or this troubled yet beautiful period in time. I wouldn't say that this was my favorite of the few Edward Yang films I have seen so far but to be fair that's a pretty high bar and this is still a remarkably beautiful film and definitely worth the time investment.

i could spend thousands of words musing on the technical details of this film such that it would probably be tantamount to me just describing eighty percent of the key shots and saying “isn’t that excellent?” and make for a pretty boring review but i’ll highlight a couple broader things which is that 1. i find the way yang works with darkness and natural light incredibly effective and compelling and 2. ive maybe never seen a movie with more command of its frame throughout. my viewing experience was probably minutely hampered by watching this with someone who’d seen and loved it prior such that the inevitability of the final ninety minutes (which was palpable regardless) was really heightened by the body language of my compatriot and a (small) measure of the surprise that the film can bank on for effect was poured out. (apologies for the digression but while i’m here i’m starting to grow a bit weary of the project of devising Perfect or particularly apt watching experiences for certain films, not that i’m ungrateful for the four–six i’ve had in the last twelve months [itself a remarkable number] but more that they’re starting to feel a touch contrived in a slightly subtractive way and i think that’s mostly because i get less joy out of organizing them than experiencing them/being surprised by them.) i think that inevitability represented my biggest problem with the writing here, that the whole film felt so intensely prefigured post-honey’s demise (down to looking at the poster after and going “oh yeah Obviously that was going to go down” or the fact that the direct translation of the title is quite a bit more literal than its english-market title) while also seeming to bank on feints and sleights (thinking of ming’s gunshot specifically) so much so that i was filled with an awful and subsuming dread for the whole run up to si’r and ming’s last scene together. there’s a certain revelatory light missing from this (either in the construction and reveal of the denouement itself or in the falling action; the thing i find so striking about anna karenina is that the Huge Prefigured Demise happens relatively early and then there’s still hundreds of pages left within which so much of the book’s beauty lies) that i Struggle with and find difficult at times. i think that lack corroborates what yang seems to be getting at in honey’s novel monologue, though, which is appreciable even if it also creates in the aggregate a film i feel incapable of seeing as Perfect as much as its most glimmering moments may make me want to see it. i think all told i left this incredibly impressed by the scale at which yang is able to pull all of this off, but there’s a similar struggle in its approaching infinity/permanence that i felt with céline and julie that both gives the film its sticky longevity and reveals its nagging flaws. certainly a testament to the massive successes of 19th century novels, even if its knee-bending in that regard sets up a standard to which it can never attain (perhaps because the feature film as a medium cannot? jury’s out) but not uninspiring at all. so much will stick in my brain forever (i find myself increasingly thinking about ming and honey ough jesus) and i think every filmmaker should aspire to this level of self-seriousness and intentionality in their work, a thing that feels sorely lacking in this century. and yes i cried for twenty minutes and had a nightmarish next six hours going directly to a birthday party. the kind of rating that may change after i watch yi yi , but i think i need a few months (at least) before i get around to that. some of my favorite moments of diegetic music in any movie that “angel baby” cover really has my heart

A brighter summer day is a 4 hour coming of age film that uses the gradual unfolding of life to build an emotionally resonant picture of adolescence. Set in a societally tense environment, it follows a boy named Si’r as he navigates school, family, and relationship pressures. The film is never driven by twists or turns, but driven by small parts that gain weight and accumulate into a grander picture. Interactions in the classroom, uncomfortable moments of authority, and shifting dynamics within cliques all lead into a sense of unease throughout the film that is bordering the line of subtlety. The overarching structure to embodies life, with a messy, indirect, and shaped directly to what’s expressed. You see the character of Si’r change but you only notice when he’s changed to much as he’s molded by the environment around him instead of dictating his own path. One of the themes of this story is the school system and how it shapes crucial events within the story, as well as being a microcosm for society in Taipei as a whole. It is shown to be rigid, hierarchal, and impersonal, prioritizing discipline over growth. The students are meant to follow standards, yet never receive guidance to becoming “functional”. Themes like generational divide are reinforced with teachers being authority figures that are often disconnected from the realities of these kids lives. It all comes together into the point of the school system being a source of pressure rather than an empathetic system meant to help children find meaning and support. It supports power over the needs of the youth, and is a critique of institutions focused on control. This films depth emerges naturally from the multitude of events that occur. It builds off the idea of loss of innocence, portrayed not as a quick shift, but a slow almost unperceived process that can’t be recognized until it’s too late. Si’r progresses through the story with his experiences gradually destroying any sense of simplicity within his life, and instead replaces it with constant conflict. This connects with themes of identity as the characters are constantly in a fight to find themselves within an environment that prioritizes expectations over personal desire. Everything around them tells them what they should be in differing ways which causes a constant pull that will eventually break them. Another key theme is social pressure and environment. It insinuates that behavior can not be separated from its context. Societal instability, and peer dynamics all play a role in shaping actions and thought, emphasizing the importance of environment in what we do. It is further deepened by the political and cultural uncertainty which although subtle, they seep into the background of the story and create constant tension. The filmmaking is impeccable with how these themes are portrayed. Edward Yang uses a very restrained, and observational style to allow the story to unfold with a sense of patience. The consistent use of long takes with minimal editing allows an almost hypnotic engagement, with constant details in the back for viewers to catch and draw conclusions from. It allows for a sense of authenticity that deepens the impact of the experiences. Visually this movie is a marvel, as it reinforces its themes with characters framed in crowded or enclosed spaces that emphasize confinement, and lack of freedom. Even in the open the camera work makes characters feel small which help allude to the idea of larger forces in play. The camera never gets personal, and instead stays at a distance where you are able to observe, reinforcing the feeling of isolation. The lighting is also used in very unique ways to highlight moral and emotional ambiguity, such as highlighting a face partially to represent a kind of “gray area”. The sound design is also impeccable as it reinforces realism with constant silence, and ambience instead of a typical score. It allows the film to breathe and gives weight to dialogue and performances by the actors. When the music is present however, it is introduced naturally as a part of the world rather than being imposed onto the film. Performances by the actors as well were exceptional at capturing its feelings of isolation, as well as vulnerability without ever feeling exaggerated or underplayed. This film seamlessly brings everything together into one cohesive and immersive story. It never offers easy answers or explanation, but instead presents a picture of growing up in an age of uncertainty and pressure that allows you to discover everything contained within it. Its length (although daunting) is iffy at times imo, but is absolutely necessary to establish connection the characters, and the story’s themes which helps make the impact feel earned. All in all this films stands as a powerful exploration of youth and the forces which shape it. Through its masterful direction it captures the often invisible struggles of adolescence that feels prevalent to not just the period, but the modern day as well. It’s a work that doesn’t stay in your mind due to spectacle, but instead relies on its honesty, patience, and ability to reveal complexity within the ordinary. An absolute masterpiece that must be watched even if the first few hours can be tough.

Only Edward Yang could make four hours feel like the only honest length for a movie about growing up under martial law, and it's a little maddening that "long" is still the first word people reach for. Yes, it's long. It's also a movie about what happens to a kid's sense of time when every institution in his life, school, family, the state, has already decided how his hours get spent without asking him. Almost none of the men in this film have real power, only fear, handed down from above and taken out on whoever's below. Fathers get interrogated by the state, then come home to interrogate their sons. I recognized this machinery of surveillance and disappearance from recent Brazilian films, Secret Agent and I’m Still Here , working through their own military dictatorship, state fear turns out to look remarkably similar no matter the hemisphere. The pattern runs all the way down until there's nobody left for Si'r's generation to pass it to, so the kids turn violence on each other instead, rebuilding the same hierarchy inside their own gangs. Which is where the baseball bats come in. The school starts requiring them to be registered, specifically because kids keep using them as weapons, the kind of fix that solves the object and ignores the reason for it. Yang's camera treats all of this the same way— at a remove. Wide shots, kids staged deep in the frame, whole scenes lit by a single bulb or a flashlight. The distance reads as cold and observational, but that's exactly what lets you see clearly, the mundane texture of these kids' daily lives sitting right next to state violence and gang violence, filmed with identical detachment. The gangs, for their part, have the full James Dean thing going, Americana rock and roll swagger borrowed wholesale from Elvis and imported into 1960s Taipei. But the look is aspirational Americana, and the weapons, when they finally show up, are something else entirely, real Japanese swords stashed in the attics of houses these families inherited from the Japanese occupiers. The thing these kids escalate to killing each other with isn't homegrown at all, it's leftover colonial hardware from an entirely different empire, discovered by accident in the walls of their own homes. The irony writes itself. Kids performing an American identity, fighting with Japanese steel, inside a Taiwan still trying to work out an identity distinct from mainland China. And caught in the middle of all of it is Ming, who barely gets to exist as her own person in this movie. Every boy who orbits her, Honey, Sly, eventually Si'r, reads her as a scoreboard rather than a human being, proof of standing. It's hard to watch in 2026 without thinking of Adolescence and the vocabulary that show put into wide circulation, boys taught to experience a girl's independence as a personal insult, her attention as a debt she owes rather than a gift she gives. Sixty-some years and a different hemisphere apart, and it's the same rot: take away a boy's sense of power everywhere else, and he'll go looking for it in the one place he's still been told he's allowed to have some. Si'r doesn't start the film as one of those boys. He ends it as exactly one, and the tragedy isn't that he snapped, it's that everything around him had been building toward that ending all along, a blow meant for someone else finding Ming instead. It didn’t move me the way Yi Yi does, but that's a high bar for anyone, including Yang himself. And yet, this is a spectacle on the scale of Leone's Once Upon a Time in America , the kind of thing very few directors can actually pull off.

Edward Yang captures 1960s Taipei and a huge ensemble with an almost unbelievable level of detail. After a while, the film stops feeling like a reconstruction of the period at all. The night school, street gangs, family homes, friendships, rivalries, romances and American pop songs do not merely provide a backdrop. They form an entire society that these children are trying to understand while the adults around them are still struggling to find their own place within it. Taiwan is changing, but nearly everyone seems caught between worlds. The parents carry the insecurity of having fled mainland China, and their children inherit that anxiety without fully understanding its source. They turn toward Elvis, movies, romantic fantasies and gangs, borrowing identities wherever they can find them. Some of the things the teenagers say sound startlingly mature, but it never feels written for effect. They have simply been forced to absorb the disappointments, fears and contradictions of the adults around them far too early. At almost four hours, the film is enormous without feeling inflated. Yang gives every relationship enough time to develop until even a passing interaction seems connected to something larger. When violence arrives, it is not exciting or cathartic. It is sudden, confused and frightening, often obscured rather than displayed. It is about as far from stylized, Tarantino-like spectacle as violence can get. It hurts because Yang has spent hours making these people and their world feel real. What happens near the end left me stunned. Learning that Yang based the film on a murder he remembered from his own childhood made it even more heartbreaking. Beneath the epic scale is the story of young people shaped, and eventually destroyed, by forces they barely comprehend. This is Edward Yang at the height of his powers, and a very close second to Yi Yi for me.

A Brighter Summer Day se estrenó en 1991, cuatro años después de que la dictadura del Kuomintang (KMT) en Taiwán levantase la ley marcial y su correspondiente censura, lo que marcó el camino hacia la democratización del país. Este es uno de los motivos por los que la obra de Edward Yang es de una enorme importancia, ya que se sitúa en un enclave histórico crucial: los años previos y posteriores a la caída de dicho régimen. En esta película, que está ambientada entre 1959 y 1961, Yang nos ofreció una mirada muy personal y crítica del KMT, que se representa en una secuencia que muestra la crueldad de aquella dictadura. Asimismo, en el film también se aprecia una considerable presencia militar, reflejo del clima de tensión provocado tras la Segunda Crisis del Estrecho de Taiwán (agosto-septiembre de 1958), que enfrentó a la República Popular de China con la República de China (Taiwán). En consecuencia, esta situación dificultó aún más la vida de los taiwaneses, que convivieron en un clima de violencia e incertidumbre. Por consiguiente, los tanques y las prácticas militares fueron habituales en ciudades como Taipéi. Esta realidad se hace presente en varios momentos de la película. Por ejemplo, en una escena diurna protagonizada por Ming y Si’r, en la que las maniobras del ejército son el contrapunto de sus devaneos juveniles. En otra escena nocturna, los tanques pasan impasibles delante de ellos. Así, la puesta en escena resalta la tensión entre la cotidianidad de los habitantes y la amenaza de los conflictos bélicos. Uno de los resultados de la presencia militar estadounidense fue la música de la emisora de las Fuerzas Armadas. Por ello, el rock ‘n’ roll de The Platters, The Beatles o Elvis Presley llegó a la vida social de los taiwaneses, siendo Elvis el eje central por el que orbitan algunos de los personajes. Una inspiración que se traslada hasta su vestimenta, debido a que algunas de sus prendas guardan similitudes con la moda del rock estadounidense (por ejemplo, la combinación de camiseta blanca con las mangas remangadas y vaqueros). Además, el título de la película deriva de un verso de una canción de Elvis llamada Are You Lonesome Tonight? . Para Yang, esta canción tenía dos significados: uno era la nueva esperanza, la libertad… y el otro era el misterio, que, como afirmó, continuaba en él. En varias ocasiones, Yang nos muestra cómo los protagonistas organizaban espectáculos para interpretar las canciones del rock ‘n’ roll estadounidense (y sobre todo de Elvis) ayudados por las transcripciones de quienes estudiaban inglés. De este modo, reflejó cómo los jóvenes buscaron consuelo en la expresión musical, a pesar de vivir en un contexto histórico marcado por la represión y la guerra. Artículo completo Vídeo completo

I don't know what it is about stories involving middle school kids being impacted by failing institutions or what exactly makes them so captivating. All I know is that both this film and Season 4 of The Wire are my favorite forms of media to ever fit in that category, even if they feel completely different from each other. I guess what makes A Brighter Summer Day stand out is that while it predates The Wire with taking a strictly blunt and more objective approach in showing how children are being funneled into criminal behavior, it still treats warm nostalgia, yearning and innocence as huge parts of its identity. All while still tackling such a disturbing real-life story involving middle school kids. It makes for such a harrowing, yet beautiful contrast throughout the movie. All in all, A Brighter Summer Day was a very emotionally heavy film, especially given its 4 hour run time. It didn't make me cry, but it left me feeling cold and empty by the end. It taps into a unique point in our childhoods, a point in time in our youth where we become more aware or privy to the grimmer parts of everyday life. It weighs in on that weird feeling where we realize the world isn't quite what we thought it was and how experiencing that at such a young age can have rippling effects throughout our lives. I'd like to believe that's what Edward Yang wanted to aim for when making this film, especially when he grew up around the same time and political climate that the film depicts. Apologies if I sound like a huge downer, but you know a film is special when it takes you to places like this and you just feel like talking about it. Overall, I loved A Brighter Summer Day. I had seen a few of Edward Yang’s films and remember catching his magnum opus, Yi Yi, back in the early 2000s. For years, I tried to get a copy of A Brighter Summer Day, but it was only available in bad prints or terrible VHS transfers. So when the American Cinematheque screened a 4K restoration in Los Angeles, I jumped at the chance to see it on the big screen - and it paid off wonderfully. This film packs a punch. Its ending is terrifying, surprising, and deeply affecting. Despite its nearly four-hour running time, it leaves you wanting more. The main character is a teenager attending night school - I’m terrible with character names - but the movie’s true subject is the entire community around him: his family, including a father, mother, and older sister who each leave a strange and lasting impression; the members of his gang; and, naturally, the lovely teenage girl at the center of his world. I won’t spoil what happens, but the ending is so shocking that it leaves you breathless. The narrative sprawls, yet every part of it feels incredibly calibrated. There are no catchy lines, but there are countless indelible moments that stay with you long after the credits roll. Near the midpoint, a terrifying sequence of violence makes you think the film has reached its climax—but it’s only the midpoint, a choice that reveals just how masterfully the narrative has been constructed. Do yourself a favor: watch this film. Start it early, and watch it in one sitting. It’s a transformative experience.

Edward Yang consegue captar com perfeição a decadência não só de uma juventude, mas de uma nação inteira traumatizada pela história. Xiao Si'r é o protagonista perfeito para mostrar a situação de Taipei nos anos 60, é um jovem inocente, porém não é um jovem perfeito, principalmente na escola, isso leva ele à sua relação com as gangues e à violência local. Quando Xiao Si'r conhece Ming, isso acaba mudando um pouco ele, tenta focar em protegê-la, porém Ming é uma pessoa instável, ela procura se relacionar com diversos homens, mentindo várias vezes a Xiao Si'r, logo isso se torna um motivo para ele adentrar mais a esse mundo, e tudo o que ele passou culmina na violência se alastrando mais e mais, tanto em Xiao Si'r quanto nas pessoas em sua volta. Um exemplo disso é seu pai, que durante todo o filme tenta educá-lo, mas aos poucos percebe que seus esforços não são suficientes e que já perdeu o controle sobre o filho. Essa relação entre pai e filho também representa muito bem o conflito entre uma geração traumatizada pelo passado e outra que está crescendo em uma sociedade completamente diferente. No fim, A Brighter Summer Day é uma joia do Novo Cinema Taiwanês, um filme que de longe pode ser apenas um longa adolescente, mas é um filme extremamente pesado sobre a violência e as consequências dela em uma geração assolada por seu passado.

Antes de mais nada, gostaria de dizer que considero uma conquista pessoal na minha cinefilia ter assistido a este filme de Edward Yang — tendo em vista a sua linguagem desafiadora e o ritmo contemplativo que a obra impõe. Na primeira vez em que tentei assistir, acabei desistindo e não voltei por um tempo; hoje, venho aqui após ter digerido e assistido à obra por completo. Já começo fazendo uma observação que me veio à mente ao terminar o longa: de certa maneira, Um Dia Quente de Verão me lembra o livro Guerra e Paz, de Liev Tolstói. Assim como Tolstói usa as Guerras Napoleônicas e a vida da aristocracia russa para expor o nascimento de uma “consciência nacional russa”, Edward Yang utiliza um crime real ocorrido em 1961 para documentar a dolorosa gênese da identidade taiwanesa moderna. Famílias, escolas e as tensões entre gangues de adolescentes criam um ambiente opressor de violência — um verdadeiro microcosmo da instabilidade sociopolítica de um país em formação. O protagonista, Xiao Si’r, encarna em si mesmo uma nação inteira perdendo a sua inocência. Graças à Nova Onda de Taiwan (a partir dos anos 1980), cineastas como Edward Yang conseguiram conectar todo esse peso do contexto histórico à vida cotidiana (algo que me remeteu ao mestre Yasujiro Ozu, por exemplo). Seus planos longos e o ritmo contemplativo muito evidente nos transportam para o berço de Taiwan nos anos 60, como se estivéssemos ali, presenciando uma nação se formar e descobrindo quais caminhos ela iria tomar. É o filme de uma vida inteira; da juventude à vida adulta de milhares de pessoas em uma ilha. Uma sociedade que, naquele momento, era marcada pela guerra, pelas rivalidades, pela influência americana (Hollywood e Elvis Presley) e pela forte presença militar em cada canto. A violência que permeia a obra não nasce do acaso, mas sim do contexto em que esses garotos se encontram; em uma sociedade taiwanesa tão instável, a violência parece ser o único caminho a seguir. Nisso a obra se mostra bastante pesada, por entrelaçar as primeiras experiências com o amor, a amizade, a família e a aceitação a profundas marcas de incerteza e melancolia. Edward Yang, portanto, fazendo uso de toda a potência que só o cinema é capaz de entregar em obras monumentais, documenta a metamorfose completa de um país e de um adolescente que funcionam como espelhos um do outro. Um final doloroso e traumático, que nos mostra que as mudanças sociais também podem vir acompanhadas de preços altos demais a se pagar.

Four hours long, yet it feels less like watching a film and more like living inside a city, a family, and a generation. Edward Yang turns one boy's story into a portrait of an entire society caught between history and modernity. Every scene seems ordinary until you realize, hours later, how much it has revealed about loneliness, violence, love, and growing up. Few films feel this vast and this intimate at the same time. By the end, you don't feel like you've watched a movie, you feel like you've lost a place that briefly became part of your life.

Why is it 4 hours long? The pacing never felt bad, tedious, it never felt dragged, but I’m just wondering why the picture had to be four hours long. It’s like, how do you determine what scene is worth putting into the film and what’s not? So, for example, the grocery store guy gets a heart attack, that’s a scene, or a plot point. Si’r helps him. In return, grocery store guy helps Si’r’s dad get an interview with a new business person. They go out for the evening, mom and dad with the new potential business partners. Si’r takes the opportunity to take a girl out on a date. He steals his mum’s watch so that he can pawn it for some money for the date. Father comes home, finds out about the stolen watch, and beats the elder brother thinking that he’s the culprit. Si’r comes home to the sight of his father violently beating his innocent brother. This seems to be the final straw of injustice for Si’r. After this, Si’r commits to seeking ‘justice’ — revenge. Imagine that, a heart attack that occurred maybe an hour prior also has its pay-off. Let’s try another scene: Ming does a screen test and cries really naturally on camera. Near the end of the film, the director wants Si’r to help them find Ming cause she’s such a great actress, but she seems to have changed addresses. In the scene just prior, Si’r finds out that Ming has fallen in love with other guys and not just him. So Si’r feels cheated. So yes, he believes she is a great actress. Anyway, I didn’t explain that well, but even in four hours I don’t think that there is a scene that is not important. Sly comes back a changed man. Si’r gets more and more philosophical: “it’s comforting to know that people can change”. If Sly can change then he is hoping that he can change Ming. Something about War and Peace . The objects in this film are very important. The flashlight, the knife, the tape recorder, the radio, and every time has its own narrative arc, a completion. Again, nothing seems to be unimportant, everything seems to be a detail. Very, very, very impressive. A Brighter Summer Day: Cat loved to sing and kept chasing that bug. He got violent there for a bit but kept mostly to singing. He sang a cover of an Elvis song and sent Elvis the tape. Elvis got back to him and even sent a gift. It’s like, Cat made it out of this cycle of violence. You don’t have to get trapped. But Si’r did. The film being a reference to this idea — that one can escape — is ironic and painful because Si’r doesn’t manage to escape, and it’s easy to see how he got trapped.

It’s all unfair. There is still a frightened animal inside us, our cover for our inability to protect ourselves is the mask of intellectualism and belief that we cultivate as we age. Beginning in youth, peace of mind is then found in numbers, who you surround yourself with is who you are. Unconquerable threats are faced through brotherhood, faith in the family you find, and pushing boundaries to see who will follow you. But behind this romantic ideal is the natural unfairness of self interest, because who wants to pick a battle they aren’t certain they’ll win? And, of course, who wants to follow when they think they can lead? Fights are not waged head to head, but only when someone can be singled out. Cornered alone and jumped, or assaulted by superior weapons, this means of protecting yourself from the world becomes the core problem that threatens you to begin with. The gangs survive by picking on the meek and isolated, becoming the object of the fears that led them to initially band together. When fairness is pursued by the few who are wizened by the horrors of this experience, the honest become easy targets of violence for a fearful, power hungry gang. And when that self interest tears groups apart, all you are left with are the sins you acted out and the looming consequences that will find you when your friends become unreliable. These methods of self protection don’t go away with time. When you become an adult, gangs are replaced by institutions. You look for stability and security in your career, but you’re still just the sum of who you know. You’re still bound to others, so when a paranoid island government finds your friends to be dissidents, they will look for you when you’re on your own, so they can corner you and beat you into submission. Your neighbors will judge your family’s actions as marks against yourself, your family members may betray you out of fear of consequences, at the end of the day our tribal nature never dissolves. Love in this conflict-ravaged world evolves. When fear of invasion, fear of abuse, and fear of transgression against all the powers that be are the emotions that rule the mind of an isolated young girl, strong, loving bonds are an unaffordable luxury. Security comes first, and that is found by choosing the most well connected and powerful man available. This hardly pushes them out of danger, as their seemingly fickle behavior irritates the damaged egos of men who allow their hubris to sink them, and now men who feel they have nothing to lose buy into their own narratives of betrayal and lash out towards these women in retaliation. Now all you can ask yourself, when you’re sitting in the aftermath of your sin, is “what have you done for others?” More importantly, what CAN you do for others? I love Edward Yang. This movie was so raw that I don’t really know what to say outside of Yang’s message itself. Every moment is squeezed to its absolute greatest impact, and Yang’s template of multi-generational households experiencing the similar events at different stages of life hits hard every single time. It makes me really really sad that very few people will get green-lights to make 4 hour movies like this ever again. Rest in peace Edward Yang, one of the greatest filmmakers we’ve ever been blessed to witness.
